differential: Lymphoma
The combination of B symptoms (night sweats, weight loss) with fatigue and abdominal pain is a classic presentation for lymphoma.
Pancreatic cancer
Worsening abdominal pain with significant unintentional weight loss in this age group is highly suspicious for a pancreatic malignancy.
Disseminated tuberculosis
This infectious disease is a well-known mimic of malignancy, presenting with chronic constitutional symptoms including night sweats, weight loss, and abdominal pain.
Renal cell carcinoma
This malignancy can present with paraneoplastic syndromes, including fever, fatigue, and weight loss, in addition to abdominal or flank pain.
Colorectal cancer
Advanced disease can present with non-specific abdominal pain and constitutional symptoms like weight loss and fatigue due to tumor burden or anemia.
eliminated: Irritable bowel syndrome
This diagnosis is excluded by the presence of red flag symptoms such as unintentional weight loss and night sweats.
Acute cholecystitis
The four-week duration of worsening symptoms is not consistent with an acute inflammatory process.

differential: Lymphoma
The patient presents with the classic triad of B symptoms (night sweats, weight loss, fatigue), generalized lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.
Metastatic Gastric Cancer
A fixed supraclavicular (Virchow's) node is a classic sign of metastasis from an abdominal primary, such as gastric cancer, which also explains the weight loss and abdominal pain.
Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
This common leukemia in older adults typically presents with fatigue, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.
Disseminated Tuberculosis
This infectious disease can mimic malignancy by causing B symptoms, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.
Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer
This malignancy can cause abdominal pain, profound weight loss, and can metastasize to the supraclavicular lymph node.
eliminated: Infectious Mononucleosis
The patient's age, the 4-week chronicity, and the fixed nature of the lymph node make an acute viral infection highly improbable.

differential: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma
The patient's age, B symptoms (fatigue, night sweats, weight loss), splenomegaly, and widespread massive lymphadenopathy are classic for an aggressive lymphoma.
Hodgkin Lymphoma
This diagnosis is highly likely given the B symptoms and extensive, contiguous-appearing lymph node involvement (cervical, mediastinal, axillary).
Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
This is a common leukemia in this age group that presents with fatigue, generalized lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.
Metastatic Cancer
A primary solid tumor (e.g., lung, gastrointestinal) can present with B symptoms and extensive lymph node metastasis, including the supraclavicular node.
Tuberculosis (Disseminated)
This infectious disease is a well-known mimic of lymphoma, capable of causing B symptoms, splenomegaly, and widespread lymphadenopathy.
eliminated: Infectious Mononucleosis
The patient's age and the chronicity and severity of findings (fixed, massive nodes) are inconsistent with a typical acute viral infection.

differential: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)
This is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and the patient's age, B symptoms, widespread disease, and CD20-positive high-proliferation B-cell histology are all classic features.
Mantle Cell Lymphoma
This CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma often affects older men and can present in an aggressive fashion with widespread lymphadenopathy and B symptoms.
Follicular Lymphoma, Grade 3
This represents a higher-grade, aggressive form of a common CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma that can present with B symptoms and rapidly progressive disease.
Burkitt Lymphoma
This is a very aggressive CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma characterized by a high proliferative index, which is consistent with the biopsy findings.
Richter's Transformation
This diagnosis accounts for the development of an aggressive high-grade lymphoma (like DLBCL) from a pre-existing, often undiagnosed, low-grade B-cell malignancy.
eliminated: T-cell Lymphoma
The positive staining for CD20, a B-cell marker, rules out a T-cell lineage.
Hodgkin Lymphoma
The diffuse CD20 positivity on lymphocytes is inconsistent with the typical immunophenotype of classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
Metastatic Carcinoma
The biopsy showed a lymphoproliferative process, not the epithelial cells that would be found in a metastatic carcinoma.
Tuberculosis
Pathology did not show caseating granulomas and instead revealed a neoplastic process.

differential: Lymphoma

differential: Lymphoma
The combination of B symptoms (fatigue, night sweats, weight loss), rubbery supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly is a classic presentation for lymphoma.
Metastatic Cancer
A supraclavicular lymph node can represent metastasis from an unknown primary (e.g., lung, gastrointestinal), which would also explain the constitutional symptoms and abdominal pain.
Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)
This common leukemia in older adults presents with fatigue, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, closely mimicking lymphoma.
Disseminated Tuberculosis
This infection can mimic malignancy by causing B symptoms, widespread lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.
Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV/CMV)
A viral infection that can cause profound fatigue, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, although less common in this age group with this severity.
eliminated: Acute viral gastroenteritis
This would not explain the 4-week duration, night sweats, weight loss, supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly.
Cirrhosis
While it can cause splenomegaly and fatigue, it does not typically cause night sweats or the prominent, rubbery lymphadenopathy described.

differential: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

This common leukemia in older adults frequently presents with generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and constitutional symptoms.
Metastatic Cancer
Widespread lymphadenopathy can represent metastasis from a solid tumor, such as lung or gastrointestinal cancer, especially with a supraclavicular node present.
Disseminated Tuberculosis
This infectious disease is a well-known mimic of lymphoma, capable of causing B symptoms, splenomegaly, and extensive lymphadenopathy.
eliminated: Acute infectious mononucleosis

differential: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)

Mantle Cell Lymphoma, blastoid variant
This aggressive variant of a B-cell lymphoma can present with B-symptoms, extensive disease, and a high proliferative index, and is CD20 positive.
Richter's Transformation
The patient's acute presentation could represent the transformation of a pre-existing indolent B-cell leukemia/lymphoma (like CLL/SLL) into an aggressive high-grade lymphoma.
High-Grade Follicular Lymphoma
This diagnosis accounts for a typically indolent B-cell lymphoma presenting in an aggressive fashion with a high proliferative rate, consistent with the clinical picture.
Burkitt Lymphoma
This is a very aggressive B-cell lymphoma characterized by a very high proliferative index that can present with B-symptoms and widespread disease, although it is less common in this age group.
eliminated: T-cell Lymphoma

Hodgkin Lymphoma

Tuberculosis
The lymph node biopsy shows a monoclonal lymphocyte proliferation rather than the characteristic caseating granulomas of tuberculosis.
Metastatic Carcinoma
The biopsy identified a lymphoid malignancy, not epithelial cells characteristic of a carcinoma.
